tips.title: Iron, 450 °C, 200 atmospheres
tips.body: The three conditions to learn: an **iron** catalyst, about **450 °C**, about **200 atmospheres**. Each is a **compromise**, and questions almost always ask you to justify one of them.

tips.title: Nitrogen from air, hydrogen from natural gas
tips.body: **Nitrogen comes from the air**, which is about 78% nitrogen. **Hydrogen comes from natural gas**. Naming the sources is a straightforward mark that many candidates leave behind.

tips.title: Ammonia is removed by cooling
tips.body: On cooling, the **ammonia liquefies and is removed**, because it condenses at a much higher temperature than nitrogen or hydrogen. The **remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled** back through the reactor, so very little is wasted.

tips.title: The temperature is a compromise
tips.body: The forward reaction is **exothermic**, so a **lower** temperature would give a **better yield** — but the reaction would be far too **slow**. 450 °C is chosen as a compromise: a **reasonable yield at a reasonable rate**. Say "compromise" and explain both halves.

tips.title: NPK is a formulation
tips.body: An **NPK fertiliser** contains compounds of **nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium**. It is a **formulation** — a mixture of various salts blended in **appropriate percentages**, not a single compound.

steps.title: The Haber process
steps.body:
**The Haber process is used to manufacture ammonia, which can be used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers.**

**The raw materials** are **nitrogen** and **hydrogen**. The nitrogen comes from **the air**, which is roughly 78% nitrogen; the hydrogen comes from **natural gas**.

**The process.** The **purified gases** are passed over a **catalyst of iron** at a **high temperature (about 450 °C)** and a **high pressure (about 200 atmospheres)**.

Some of the hydrogen and nitrogen react to form ammonia:

$$\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\mathrm{H_2(g)} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3(g)}$$

**The reaction is reversible**, so some of the ammonia produced **breaks down** into nitrogen and hydrogen again. That is why the yield in a single pass is low.

**Separating the ammonia.** **On cooling, the ammonia liquefies and is removed.** Ammonia condenses at a much higher temperature than nitrogen or hydrogen, so cooling the mixture turns the ammonia to liquid while the other two stay as gases.

**Recycling.** **The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled** back into the reactor. This is why a low yield per pass matters far less than it first appears: the unreacted gas is not wasted, it simply goes round again.

steps.title: Why those conditions
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)*

Every condition in the Haber process is a **compromise**, and you should be able to **explain the trade-off between rate of production and position of equilibrium**.

**Pressure: high is better for yield.** The left side has $4$ gas molecules and the right has $2$. By Le Chatelier's principle, **increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer molecules** — the ammonia. Higher pressure also **increases the rate**, because the particles are closer together.

So why not use more than 200 atmospheres? Because very high pressure needs **thick, strong pipes and vessels**, which are **expensive to build and maintain**, and the **energy** to compress the gas costs money. 200 atmospheres is as high as is **economic and safe**.

**Temperature: low is better for yield, high is better for rate.** The forward reaction is **exothermic**, so raising the temperature favours the **endothermic reverse** reaction and **lowers the yield**. But a low temperature makes the reaction **far too slow** to be useful.

**450 °C is the compromise**: the yield is only moderate, but the ammonia is produced **quickly enough** to be worth making. Combined with recycling, a modest yield per pass is acceptable.

**The catalyst: rate only.** The **iron** catalyst **speeds up the reaction** so equilibrium is reached sooner, but it **does not change the position of the equilibrium** or the yield. It reduces the temperature needed for a workable rate, which saves energy.

steps.title: NPK fertilisers
steps.body:
**Compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium are used as fertilisers to improve agricultural productivity.** Plants need all three elements, and soil is gradually depleted of them as crops are harvested.

**NPK fertilisers contain compounds of all three elements.** They are **formulations** — mixtures of **various salts containing appropriate percentages** of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, blended for the crop and the soil. An NPK fertiliser is therefore not a single compound.

**Where the components come from.**

- **Ammonia** from the Haber process **can be used to manufacture ammonium salts and nitric acid**, which supply the **nitrogen**.
- **Potassium chloride** and **potassium sulfate** are obtained by **mining**, and supply the **potassium**.
- **Phosphate rock** is also **obtained by mining**, but **cannot be used directly as a fertiliser** — it is **insoluble**, so plant roots cannot take it up.

**Making the phosphate usable.** **Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid or sulfuric acid to produce soluble salts that can be used as fertilisers.** The acid used decides the product:

- with **nitric acid** → **phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate**
- with **sulfuric acid** → **single superphosphate, a mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate**
- with **phosphoric acid** → **triple superphosphate, which is calcium phosphate**

**Industrial production** of NPK fertilisers uses **a variety of raw materials in several integrated processes** — the plant makes the ammonia, the nitric acid and the treated phosphate, then blends them.

steps.title: Comparing industrial and laboratory preparation
steps.body: AQA asks you to **compare the industrial production of fertilisers with laboratory preparations of the same compounds**. The chemistry is the same; the scale and the priorities are not.

steps.text: The laboratory route is a **batch** process: set up, react, collect, clean out, start again.
steps.note: flexible but slow, and labour intensive per gram

steps.text: **Industrially**: ammonia from the Haber process is reacted with sulfuric acid **continuously**, in very large reactors.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. Name the raw materials for the Haber process and the source of each.
2. State the catalyst, temperature and pressure used.
3. Write the symbol equation for the Haber process.

**Part B.**

4. Explain how the ammonia is separated from the unreacted gases.
5. Explain why the unreacted gases are recycled.
6. Name the three elements in an NPK fertiliser.

**Part C.**

7. Explain why 450 °C is used rather than a lower temperature.
8. Explain why 200 atmospheres is used rather than a much higher pressure.
9. Name the products when phosphate rock is treated with each of nitric acid, sulfuric acid and phosphoric acid.

For questions 7 and 8, use the word **compromise** and explain both sides of it.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Quote the conditions exactly.** **iron** catalyst, about **450 °C**, about **200 atmospheres**. Vague answers such as "high temperature and pressure" score less than the numbers.

**Justify the temperature as a compromise, in both directions.** The forward reaction is **exothermic**, so a lower temperature gives a **higher yield** — but too slowly. A higher temperature gives a **faster rate** but a **lower yield**. 450 °C balances them. Give **both halves** or the mark is not earned.

**Justify the pressure by cost and safety.** Higher pressure would improve **both** yield and rate, so the limit is **not chemical**: very high pressures need **expensive, strong vessels** and a great deal of **energy** to compress the gas.

**Be precise about the catalyst.** It increases the **rate** and lets a lower temperature be used, but it has **no effect on the position of the equilibrium** or the yield. This is the single most common error in Haber questions.

**Explain the separation by condensation.** Cooling **liquefies the ammonia** because it condenses at a much higher temperature than nitrogen or hydrogen, so it can be run off while they stay gaseous.

**Link recycling to the low yield.** A single pass converts only a modest fraction, but because the unreacted gases are **recycled**, the overall conversion is high and little raw material is wasted. This is what rescues an unpromising equilibrium position.

**Say why phosphate rock is treated.** It is **insoluble**, so plants cannot absorb it; acid treatment gives **soluble salts** that they can.

**Remember NPK is a formulation.** Various salts blended in **appropriate percentages** — not one compound, and the ratio is chosen for the crop and soil.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- The **Haber process** manufactures **ammonia** for **nitrogen-based fertilisers**.
- Raw materials: **nitrogen from the air**, **hydrogen from natural gas**.
- Conditions: **iron catalyst**, about **450 °C**, about **200 atmospheres**.
- $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3}$ — **reversible**, so some ammonia breaks down again.
- **On cooling, the ammonia liquefies and is removed**; the unreacted gases are **recycled**.
- **Pressure**: high favours ammonia ($4$ molecules → $2$) and raises the rate, but is limited by the **cost of vessels and energy**.
- **Temperature**: the forward reaction is **exothermic**, so low favours yield but is too slow — **450 °C is a compromise**.
- The **catalyst changes the rate, not the position or the yield**.
- **NPK fertilisers** contain compounds of **nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium**, as a **formulation** of salts in appropriate percentages.
- **Ammonia** makes **ammonium salts and nitric acid**.
- **Potassium chloride and potassium sulfate** are **mined**.
- **Phosphate rock** is mined but is **insoluble**, so it **cannot be used directly**.
- Treated with **nitric acid** → phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate; **sulfuric acid** → single superphosphate, a mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate; **phosphoric acid** → triple superphosphate, which is calcium phosphate.

Although only a modest fraction converts each time, the **unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen are recycled** back into the reactor after the ammonia has been removed by cooling.

questions.prompt: Compare the industrial production of ammonium sulfate with its laboratory preparation.
questions.solution:
The **chemistry is the same** — ammonia reacting with sulfuric acid — but the scale and priorities differ.

In the **laboratory** it is a **batch** process: a titration establishes the exact volumes, the reaction is repeated without indicator, and the salt is crystallised. The aim is a **small, pure** sample.

**Industrially** the reaction is **continuous** and on a very large scale, using ammonia straight from the Haber process, with **several integrated processes** on one site. The aim is **large quantities at low cost**, and a blended product is acceptable.

questions.prompt:
The Haber process uses an iron catalyst, a temperature of about 450 °C and a pressure of about 200 atmospheres. The forward reaction is exothermic.

Explain how each of these conditions is chosen, referring to both the rate of production and the position of equilibrium. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
**Pressure.** The equation $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\mathrm{H_2} \rightleftharpoons 2\mathrm{NH_3}$ has **4 gas molecules on the left and 2 on the right**. By Le Chatelier's principle, **increasing the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards the side with fewer molecules**, so the **yield of ammonia rises**. Higher pressure also brings the particles closer together, so collisions are more frequent and the **rate increases** as well. Both effects favour going higher.

The limit is **practical rather than chemical**. Very high pressures require **thick, strong vessels and pipes** that are expensive to build and maintain, carry a **safety** risk, and need a great deal of **energy** to compress the gas. About **200 atmospheres** is as high as is economic and safe.

**Temperature.** The forward reaction is **exothermic**, so the system counteracts a temperature rise by favouring the **endothermic reverse** reaction. A **lower** temperature would therefore give a **higher yield** of ammonia. But at a low temperature the **rate** is far too slow to be commercially useful — a high yield produced too slowly is worthless.

**About 450 °C is a compromise**: the yield is only moderate, but the ammonia is made fast enough to be economic. Because the unreacted gases are **recycled** after the ammonia is removed by cooling, the modest yield per pass is acceptable.

**The catalyst.** The **iron** catalyst lowers the activation energy for the **forward and reverse reactions equally**, so it **increases the rate** and equilibrium is reached **sooner**. It has **no effect on the position of the equilibrium**, so the **yield is unchanged** — but by making the reaction workable at 450 °C rather than a higher temperature, it indirectly protects the yield and saves energy.

examTechnique.body:
Learn the conditions exactly: **iron catalyst, about 450 °C, about 200 atmospheres**, with **nitrogen from the air** and **hydrogen from natural gas**. The ammonia is removed by **cooling until it liquefies**, and the unreacted gases are **recycled**.

Justify the temperature as a **compromise** — lower gives a better yield, higher gives a better rate — and the pressure by the **cost of vessels and energy**. The catalyst changes the **rate only**.
examinerErrors: Giving "high temperature and pressure" instead of the values.
Saying the catalyst increases the yield.
Explaining the temperature compromise from only one side.
Claiming higher pressure would lower the yield.
Saying the ammonia is filtered rather than condensed.
Forgetting that the unreacted gases are recycled.
Using phosphate rock directly as a fertiliser.
Describing NPK as a single compound rather than a formulation.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer quotes the conditions with their values, names the source of each raw material, and justifies every condition against **both** rate and equilibrium position. It counts the gas molecules to explain the pressure effect, gives the economic and safety reasons for stopping at 200 atmospheres, presents 450 °C explicitly as a compromise with both halves stated, and insists that the catalyst changes the rate but never the yield. It links the low yield per pass to **recycling**, and treats NPK as a **formulation** whose phosphate had to be made soluble with acid.
